text: SOC 2 is the compliance word you'll hear constantly in enterprise security, and also the most loosely used one. It's not a certificate and there's no logo a company gets awarded. It's an attestation report, issued by an independent CPA firm, and what it actually examines is more specific — and more interesting — than most people realize.

The AICPA scopes every SOC 2 engagement against the Trust Services Criteria. Security is the common criteria — protection against unauthorized logical and physical access — and it's mandatory in every single SOC 2 report, no exceptions. Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy get added only when they're actually relevant: a payroll processor includes Processing Integrity, while a tool that never touches personal data can reasonably leave Privacy out of scope entirely.

Here's the distinction to know cold. A Type I report tests whether controls are suitably designed as of one specific date — would this work, if it ran as described? A Type II report tests whether those same controls actually operated that way, with sampled evidence pulled across a six-to-twelve-month review period. Type I is a snapshot of design. Type II is proof of behavior over time, and it's what serious enterprise buyers actually ask vendors for.

So what does an auditor's fieldwork actually involve? Not reading your access control policy and taking your word for it. A Type II auditor pulls a sample of real terminated employees and checks system logs for exactly when access was revoked. They pull a sample of production deployments and check for a documented approval before each one merged. And when a sample turns up an exception — access that lingered two weeks too long — that gets documented, not hidden.

That's the real shape of SOC 2: a scoped set of criteria, evidence-based testing, and an independent opinion built from actual samples rather than self-reported claims. A report with a few noted exceptions is normal and even expected; a spotless one invites more scrutiny, not less. Next lesson moves to ISO 27001 — a framework built around an entire management system you certify, not a single report an auditor hands you.
